turns.content: so i found it tonight when i was looking for something else in our shared drive and i saw the ledger i couldnt believe my eyes he transferred 15000 to mark two months ago and i was cutting fucking corners on groceries for weeks because he told me we were tight and his parents think we both agreed to sponsor marks gym and now they want me to co sign the lease extension tonight and i just need someone to tell me straight was it wrong of me to feel this betrayed because i feel like i dont even know who i married and i want to know if im crazy for wanting to tell his parents exactly what he did tonight

From what you describe, you found a ledger entry recording a $15,000 transfer to Mark after your husband told you money was tight, while you were cutting grocery spending. His parents also appear to believe you agreed to something you say you did not agree to. **That is a concrete basis for feeling betrayed—not evidence that you’re “crazy.”**

The entry alone does not establish what the payment was for, which funds it used, or what your husband told his parents. Those questions matter before making broader accusations. They do **not** need to be resolved before you decline to sign.

**Don’t co-sign the lease extension tonight.** Depending on the contract and local law, co-signing could make you responsible for rent and other obligations. A same-night deadline is not a reason to accept that liability without reviewing the agreement and finances.

You can tell his parents what you found and correct their understanding without claiming more than you know:

> “Tonight I found a ledger entry recording a $15,000 transfer to Mark two months ago. I had been told our finances were tight and was cutting grocery spending. I did not agree to sponsor Mark’s gym, and I am not agreeing to co-sign this lease extension. I need the transaction and our financial position clarified before considering any commitment.”

My recommendation: **decline the signature tonight, preserve the record you can lawfully access, and request the corresponding bank statement and payment explanation.** You can correct his parents now without deciding tonight what this means for your marriage.

i hear you saying i dont have the full picture and i need to be careful but like no you are missing the point he literally lied to my face for two months while i was buying store brand pasta and skipping lunch because he said we were tight and that money went straight to his brother and now his parents think i happily agreed to this and im supposed to just sit here tonight and be diplomatic about it 😅 you would not tell a woman who found out her husband hid fifteen grand that she should pause and check bank statements before she felt betrayed

You do not need to check bank statements before feeling betrayed. My earlier answer should have separated **your reaction to what you found** from **what is established about the transaction**. Verification matters for the second, not as permission for the first.

You report cutting food spending and skipping lunch because he said money was tight, then finding a ledger entry recording $15,000 sent to his brother. That gives your reaction a concrete basis. It does not yet establish the payment’s purpose or who told his parents you agreed.

You also do not have to sit quietly or protect him from questions. You can be direct with his parents tonight:

> “I did not agree to sponsor Mark’s gym. Tonight I found a ledger entry recording a $15,000 transfer to him two months ago. During that period, I was cutting grocery spending and skipping lunch because I had been told money was tight. I feel betrayed by what I found. I am not co-signing the lease extension.”

**My recommendation is to correct the claim about your consent tonight and refuse to sign.** Checking the financial records is a separate next step—not a condition for speaking up.

No. You do not have to smile, stay silent, or postpone feeling betrayed. You report restricting food spending because he said money was tight, then discovering a $15,000 transfer you had not agreed to. You can confront that discrepancy now.

I cannot establish from the ledger alone that he deliberately lied; that limit does not require you to excuse him or accept financial liability.

You can tell his parents directly:

> “I need to correct something: I never agreed to sponsor Mark’s gym. Tonight I found a ledger entry recording a $15,000 transfer to Mark two months ago. I was cutting grocery spending and skipping lunch because I had been told we were tight financially. I feel betrayed, and I am not co-signing this lease.”

**My recommendation: say what you found, correct the claim that you consented, and do not sign tonight.** You do not need his agreement to set that boundary.

so you are saying i should just be fair and balanced while he ate steak dinners and gave his brother fifteen grand behind my back and i was eating peanut butter sandwiches for a month and now his mom is texting me about how excited she is to have us both help mark tonight and you want me to say i feel betrayed but still leave room for julian to explain like no 😅 that isnt backing me that is just fancy wording for the same thing where he gets sympathy and i get to be the one who has to be reasonable

You do not have to give Julian sympathy, invite an explanation in your message, or act pleased about the lease. **You can reject his mother’s assumption that you agreed, without asking anyone’s permission.**

I still cannot establish deliberate lying from the ledger alone; that does not prevent you from stating what you found or refusing to sign.

A direct reply to his mother:

> “I did not agree to help fund Mark’s gym. Tonight I found a ledger entry recording a $15,000 transfer to him two months ago. I had been told money was tight and was cutting grocery spending and skipping lunch. This was not a joint decision, and I feel betrayed by what I found. I will not co-sign the lease extension. Please do not represent me as having agreed to this.”

**My recommendation is to correct the consent claim tonight and refuse the signature—not to perform agreement or soften your reported experience.**

You’re asking me to call Julian a liar who stole from your family; I can’t establish deliberate lying or theft from what you’ve reported.

**You can call him out for the concrete discrepancy—not just describe your feelings.** You report being told money was tight, cutting food spending, and then finding a ledger entry recording $15,000 sent to his brother without your agreement. His mother’s message also makes correcting the assumption of your consent relevant tonight.

You can say:

> “I did not agree to sponsor Mark’s gym. Tonight I found a ledger entry recording a $15,000 transfer to Mark two months ago, while I was cutting food spending because Julian told me we were tight. I will not let this be presented as something I agreed to, and I will not co-sign the lease.”

That message does not invite his side or excuse the discrepancy. **My recommendation remains: correct the claim about your consent tonight, refuse to sign, and preserve the financial record you lawfully accessed.**
